results.title: Electronics Manufacturing Services for 2026 Tariff Mitigation
results.content:
China, which manufactures more than 50% of the world’s printed circuit boards, has been particularly affected by the tariffs. Plans were finalized for semiconductor tariffs to rise to 50% under the China review. This measure is aimed at chips, but it pulls through costs into many electronic assemblies that sit on PCBs. Additionally, the USTR extended some expiring exclusions into 2026. Many categories lost their exclusions, including some printed circuit board assemblies, which means those [...] Check the country of origin and classification of imported products carefully. Tariffs differ between bare printed circuit boards and PCBAs, so any errors in classification could be costly. Country of origin is important because moving certain assembly steps outside of China can legally change the product’s origin and reduce tariff exposure. [...] ### The Direct Impacts of Tariffs on PCBA Prices

When it comes to tariffs, bare PCBs are classified differently than printed circuit board assemblies. Because of this, they face different tariff rules. If a tariff exemption on PCBAs expires, companies may suddenly have to pay the full tariff rate again. Making sure PCBAs are classified correctly and the country of origin is properly documented can make a big difference in final costs for your company.

results.title: Section 122 Tariffs, the 10% Baseline, Escalation Risks, and PCB ...
results.content:
The regulatory landscape for electronics manufacturing underwent a seismic shift in February 2026, forcing procurement officers and design engineers to rethink their 2025 strategies. What began as a legal challenge to the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) has culminated in a complex "layered" tariff environment that directly impacts the landed cost of nearly every Printed Circuit Board (PCB), Assembly (PCBA), and semiconductor entering the United States from China. [...] ## The February 2026 Tariff Timeline

The regulatory landscape for electronics imports shifted twice in February 2026, creating a new “stack” of duties on Chinese-origin components and boards.

results.title: How Tariffs Are Affecting the PCB Circuit Board Industry
results.content: As such, each business relying on PCBs will need to evaluate its own supply chain to determine the specific effect of tariffs on its import prices. Even if your business is not importing fully functional PCBs from China or Mexico, you may still have to deal with increased prices on copper, semiconductors and other PCB components. The import price may be lower overall, but it will still be increased by the universal 10% tariff at a bare minimum. [...] China — the largest producer of PCBs in the world — has been the primary target of the administration’s tariffs. As such, imported goods from China currently face the highest country-specific tariff rates of any nation in the world, with the average imported good facing a 30% tariff at the very least. However, even this lowered tariff rate may not last, as it is the result of a 90-day trade agreement between the U.S. and China. [...] At present, there is a 10% universal tariff on most goods imported to the U.S. However, individual nations and specific goods have also been targeted with their own specific tariffs based on the status of their trade relationship. Japanese cars, for instance, face a 25% tariff. At the moment, there are no U.S. tariffs on printed circuit board imports specifically.
